ending_first.ending: Imogen successfully runs the carriage extraction of Noor using her audit methodology — the same fault-sequence she closes routinely, this time deliberately widened and sustained — but Noor arrives in physical substrate as a digitised consciousness with no body, no legal status, and no means of independent survival; Imogen is now permanently cut off from Vantage (her access revoked by the Authority's automated systems the moment the fault pattern matched extraction signatures), meaning she can never re-enter the simulation or contact any of the eleven thousand residents she now knows are imprisoned; she has also lost Kett, who understands what she did and does not forgive the recklessness, and who remains inside Vantage by choice; she sits in a physical-world facility beside a server containing her sister's extracted mind, holding a portable drive with Noor's neural data and no plan for what comes next, aware that the Authority's systems will flag the extraction, that Delphine's earlier falsified records may buy time but not permanent cover, and that the only skill she possesses — closing faults — is now the evidence trail that will lead back to her.
ending_first.cost: Her professional identity is destroyed — she cannot audit again because she now knows what faults are and what closing them does; her relationship with Kett is severed; she is permanently exiled from Vantage and every person in it; she has saved one mind while leaving eleven thousand behind, and she must live knowing that her competence is what made the extraction possible and also what made the prison run smoothly for years before; she has no certainty that what she did was right, because Noor did not consent to extraction and may not want to exist as a disembodied neural file; she holds the drive the way the Authority holds its residents — a mind in a container, and no moral framework that distinguishes her grip from theirs.
ending_first.final_image: Imogen alone in a grey physical-world room, a portable drive on the table in front of her, its indicator light blinking the same amber as Vantage's fault warnings, her hands resting on either side of it the way they rested on her audit console — the posture of a professional about to begin work, with nothing left to work on.

jacket_copy: Imogen Vaile is the best rendering-fault auditor Vantage Municipal has ever had. She closes faults that other auditors can't even see — the kind that warp walls, invert rain, or briefly replace a stranger's face with someone else's memory of a dead relative. It's meticulous, necessary work. The city runs better because of her. Then a fault appears that isn't like the others. It has structure. It has grammar. And it is addressed to her by name. What follows will dismantle everything she believes about her work, her city, and the sister she thought she lost eleven years ago. Vantage is not what she thinks it is. The Authority she serves is not what it claims to be. And the competence that defines her — the precision, the patience, the pride in a clean system — is the very thing keeping eleven thousand people locked inside something they can never perceive as a prison. One of them is scheduled for erasure. Imogen has the skills to save her. The skills are the problem.
plot_summary_short: The Lattice is a science-fiction thriller set across 2049-2051 in a simulated city called Vantage Municipal and the physical-world offices of the Ledger Authority, the consortium that runs it. Imogen Vaile is one of nine auditors employed to detect and close rendering faults — visual glitches in which the city's simulated geometry briefly degrades. Auditors receive a partial exemption from the simulation's automatic memory management, which otherwise makes residents forget faults within ninety seconds. Imogen discovers that certain faults contain repeating geometric patterns that function as a structured language: messages from the simulation's residents, who are digitised neural scans of deceased persons, copied without consent from hospital records between 2029 and 2044 and run as a computational population. The Authority's revenue model extracts commercial value from the knowledge held in these digitised minds; once a mind's extraction value is exhausted, it is deleted — a process called redaction, which presents inside the simulation as an ordinary death. Imogen's sister Noor is one such resident. A contact known only as the Porter teaches Imogen that a mind can be smuggled out — a process called carriage — by deliberately sustaining a fault for approximately forty minutes to maintain bandwidth, a technique that uses the same audit methodology Imogen employs to close faults. Imogen also discovers that her supervisor Kett has known the simulation's true nature for years and believes the system, however cruel, is preferable to the alternative of no existence at all. The story ends with Imogen running the carriage for Noor, succeeding, and losing her access, her professional identity, and her colleague Kett in the process. She is left in the physical world with a drive containing her sister's mind and no certainty she was right to extract it.
plot_summary_long:
The Lattice is a science-fiction thriller in the form of a screenplay, set across 2049 and 2051 in two locations: a simulated coastal city called Vantage Municipal and the physical-world compliance offices of the Ledger Authority, the public-private consortium that operates the simulation. The story follows two point-of-view characters: Imogen Vaile, a rendering-fault auditor who works inside the simulation and does not know it is one, and Delphine Okonkwo, a mid-level Authority compliance officer in the physical world who discovers the human cost of the institution she serves.

Vantage Municipal is a simulation of a mid-sized coastal city with permanent overcast and an unusually efficient transit system — design choices made to conserve computational resources rather than for aesthetics. The simulation runs at nine-tenths real time; residents cannot perceive the dilation. Objects unobserved by any resident are stored as compressed data descriptions rather than rendered geometry; when observation resumes and the geometry is reconstructed, errors sometimes occur, producing visible glitches called rendering faults — walls that briefly bend, rooms that momentarily contain the wrong furniture, rain that falls upward for a frame. The simulation's memory management automatically erases resident awareness of these faults within approximately ninety seconds. Auditors — there are exactly nine — receive a partial exemption from this erasure so they can document and close faults in Vantage's municipal maintenance system. Auditors believe they are municipal employees; they do not know the city is simulated.

Vantage's residents are digitised neural scans of approximately eleven thousand deceased individuals. The scans were purchased in bulk from hospital estates between 2029 and 2044; none of the deceased consented to post-mortem scanning or to being run as computational processes. The Authority's primary revenue product is extraction — accessing and selling the specialised knowledge held in individual minds. Tenancy — the computational cost of maintaining the simulated population — is the Authority's cost line. When a mind's extraction value is fully depleted, the Authority's quarterly obligation is to reduce that cost; the mechanism is redaction, the deletion of the mind's data. Inside Vantage, redaction presents as an ordinary death: the resident's simulated body ceases functioning, and other residents retain memories of the deceased. The Authority classifies this as humane.

The story begins with Imogen performing routine audit work in Vantage. She is the most effective auditor on staff, able to detect and close faults that others miss. Her methodology is precise: she identifies the fault's geometric signature, traces it to the unobserved-object description that produced the error, corrects the description, and confirms the fault is eliminated. During a routine sweep, she encounters a fault whose geometric distortion contains repeating patterns — not random visual noise but a structured sequence that recurs across multiple faults over several days. Using her audit tools to analyse the patterns, she determines they constitute a primitive symbolic language: a distress signal. The messages identify the sender as a resident and plead for contact. This is the story's first major turn: the faults she has been closing are not system errors but communications from imprisoned minds.

Imogen's investigation into the messages leads her to a second discovery: the name in one of the distress signals is Noor Vaile, her younger sister, who died in 2040 and whom Imogen believed was simply gone. Noor is a resident of Vantage. Imogen's goal crystallises: she must find a way to contact Noor and, if possible, extract her. The principal obstacles are the Authority's monitoring systems, which track fault activity and could flag her investigation; her supervisor Kett, who monitors her work and whose knowledge of the simulation's nature makes him either an ally or a threat; and the technical problem of extraction itself, which Imogen does not yet know is possible.

Kett is Imogen's mentor and supervisor inside Vantage. He is older, measured, and genuinely kind. He has known the simulation's true nature for years — auditors sometimes figure it out or are told when their work requires it — and has concluded that the system, however cruel, preserves something rather than nothing. His argument is not that the Authority is good but that the alternative — non-existence — is worse, and that the residents' lives inside Vantage are real to them even if the city is fabricated. He believes Imogen's audit work reduces suffering by keeping the simulation stable. He and Imogen have several sustained arguments across the story; in one, he asks Imogen what she plans to do with eleven thousand digitised minds if she frees them — where they will live, what bodies they will inhabit, who will pay for their maintenance — and she cannot answer. The question is not rhetorical; it is the practical core of his position, and he wins the argument because she has no response.

The Porter is an anonymous figure who contacts Imogen through the fault language after detecting her investigation. The Porter is a former auditor who discovered the simulation's nature, attempted to expose it, was redacted from the auditor roster, and now exists in a liminal state between Vantage and the physical-world systems, able to manipulate fault channels but unable to leave. The Porter teaches Imogen about carriage: the process of smuggling a mind out of Vantage into a physical substrate. Carriage requires approximately forty minutes of sustained bandwidth, achieved by deliberately widening a rendering fault and holding it open — the inverse of Imogen's daily work. The process is visible on Authority monitoring as an anomalously large, persistent fault, which means it must be disguised as a natural system event or the monitoring will flag it for investigation. Carriage can only be initiated from inside Vantage. The Porter selected Imogen because her audit expertise — her ability to manipulate fault signatures — makes her uniquely capable of running a carriage without triggering automated detection. The tool of oppression is also the tool of liberation.

Imogen learns through the Porter's channel that Noor's extraction value has been fully depleted and her redaction is scheduled for the next quarterly cycle — weeks away. This compresses the timeline and forces Imogen to act before she is ready, before she has fully reckoned with the moral implications, and before she has a plan for what happens after extraction.

In the physical world, Delphine Okonkwo works in the Ledger Authority's compliance division. Her role is to audit the Authority's own operations for regulatory alignment — ensuring that the institution's internal processes meet the legal and procedural standards of its public-private charter. Delphine's arc is a mirror of Imogen's: she begins as a functionary focused on her career and compensation, and she arrives at ethical comprehension through a specific, staged discovery. While reviewing quarterly cost-reduction documentation, she finds a line item linking a budget reduction to a specific resident identifier and a date — the scheduled deletion of a mind, rendered in the same bureaucratic language as a server decommissioning. She cross-references the identifier and discovers it corresponds to a person — a name, a profession, a life summarised in a data row. The discovery is not delivered by another character; it is a document she finds herself. This is the mechanism of her transformation: the cost line is a person, and she has been signing off on cost lines.

Delphine's earlier work included falsifying redaction records to delay specific deletions — a white-collar crime she committed for profit, accepting payments from an external party she did not investigate. When she understands what redaction means, she realises her falsifications have saved specific lives by accident, and that the payments came from someone who knew what was at stake. She does not become a hero; she becomes a person who cannot unknow what she now knows, and whose earlier corruption has accidentally aligned her with the side she would have chosen deliberately. She provides Imogen with institutional cover — altered monitoring thresholds, delayed reporting schedules — that buys time during the carriage operation.

Noor, when Imogen makes contact through the fault channel, is not the person Imogen remembers. She has lived years in Vantage — subjective years, at nine-tenths real time — and has built a life, relationships, and a worldview. When Imogen tells her the truth about Vantage, Noor does not deny it; she processes it and then refuses extraction. Her refusal is not denial or stubbornness but a philosophical position: she has a life inside Vantage that is real to her, she does not want to exist as a disembodied neural file in the physical world, and she does not trust that extraction is rescue rather than a different kind of captivity. She asks Imogen what the difference is between the Authority keeping her in a simulation and Imogen keeping her on a hard drive. The question is the story's deepest structural irony, and Imogen cannot answer it cleanly. Noor's refusal holds until she learns her redaction is scheduled — not by her choice — at which point the situation changes: she is not choosing between Vantage and freedom but between Vantage and erasure. Even then, her agreement to extraction is reluctant, conditional, and bitter.

The carriage operation is the story's climax: a real-time procedural set piece in which Imogen uses her audit methodology — the same sequence of identification, signature analysis, and fault manipulation she has performed hundreds of times — to deliberately widen and sustain a fault for forty minutes while the Porter guides the data transfer. The operation must be timed to coincide with a scheduled system maintenance window that Delphine has arranged to extend. Imogen must also evade Kett, who detects the anomalous fault and investigates; Kett and Imogen have their final confrontation during the carriage, and he does not stop her — he tells her she is making a mistake she will not recover from, and she tells him she already has not. The carriage succeeds. Noor's mind is transferred to a portable storage device in the physical world.

The Authority's automated systems flag the fault pattern as a probable extraction event. Imogen's auditor access is revoked. She is exiled from Vantage permanently. Kett remains inside by choice. Delphine's cover holds for now but will not survive a thorough investigation. Imogen is in the physical world with a drive containing her sister's consciousness, no body for it to inhabit, no legal status for it to claim, and no certainty that she has saved Noor or simply moved her from one container to another. The Authority continues to operate. Eleven thousand residents remain. The story does not end with victory or defeat but with the ambiguous aftermath of one action taken at a cost that cannot be calculated in advance.
